items.item: A vector clock keeps one counter per process, incremented on its own events and merged by element-wise maximum on message receipt.

at.step: Reveal: one counter per process, merged by the largest value seen

items.item: One vector dominates another exactly when every entry is greater than or equal and at least one is strictly greater; this holds exactly when the first event happened-before the second.

at.step: Reveal: one counter per process, merged by the largest value seen

items.item: Two vectors where neither dominates the other are concurrent; unlike a scalar clock, a vector clock detects this exactly, with no false positives or negatives.

at.step: Predict: which version does the store keep?

items.item: A version vector is the same mechanism applied to versions of one data item at the replicas that have coordinated a write to it, rather than to events at processes in general.

at.step: Reveal: the same rule, pointed at a replica instead of a process

items.item: Dynamo surfaces concurrent, causally unrelated versions to the application via get(), with a context the application must return on put() to supersede the versions it reconciled.

at.step: Reveal: the Dynamo example, five versions, one real trace

items.item: Dynamo truncates its vector clocks past a fixed number of entries (named as ten) by dropping the oldest pair, which can cause a genuinely ordered pair of versions to be mistaken for concurrent.

at.step: Prove it: can truncating a vector make an ordered pair look concurrent?

items.item: Siblings are concurrent, unmerged versions a store returns together when neither dominates; allow_mult controls whether a store creates them or falls back to last-write-wins.

at.step: Reveal: siblings, and the setting that lets them multiply

items.item: A plain vector clock cannot distinguish two concurrent updates coordinated by the same replica, since both bump that replica's entry identically; this is the root cause of sibling explosion under duplicate or out-of-order delivery.

at.step: Reveal: the dot that tells two writes apart

items.item: A dotted version vector adds a single event identifier (a dot) to a version vector's context, letting updates with an identical underlying vector still be told apart, bounding sibling growth to genuine concurrency.
